{{Short description|Set-theoretic concept}}
In [[set theory]], a '''Grothendieck universe''' is a set <math>U</math> with the following properties:

# If <math>x</math> is an element of <math>U</math> and if <math>y</math> is an element of <math>x</math>, then <math>y</math> is also an element of <math>U</math>. (<math>U</math> is a [[transitive set]].)
# If <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> are both elements of <math>U</math>, then <math>\{x,y\}</math> is an element of <math>U</math>.
# If <math>x</math> is an element of <math>U</math>, then <math>\mathcal{P}(x)</math>, the [[power set]] of <math>x</math>, is also an element of <math>U</math>.
# If <math>\{x_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in I}</math> is a family of elements of <math>U</math>, and if {{mvar|I}} is an element of <math>U</math>, then the union <math display=inline>\bigcup_{\alpha\in I} x_\alpha</math> is an element of <math>U</math>.

A Grothendieck universe is meant to provide a set in which all of mathematics can be performed. In fact, [[uncountable]] Grothendieck universes provide [[model theory|models]] of set theory with the natural ∈-relation, natural power set operation, etc. Elements of a Grothendieck universe are sometimes called '''small sets'''. The idea of universes is due to [[Alexander Grothendieck]], who used them as a way of avoiding [[proper class]]es in [[algebraic geometry]]. Grothendieck’s original proposal was to add the following '''axiom of universes''' to the usual axioms of set theory: For every set <math>s</math>, there exists a universe <math>U</math> that contains <math>s</math>, i.e., <math>s \in U</math>.

The existence of a nontrivial Grothendieck universe goes beyond the usual axioms of [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory]]; in particular it would imply the existence of [[Inaccessible cardinal|strongly inaccessible cardinals]]. [[Tarski–Grothendieck set theory]] is an axiomatic treatment of set theory, used in some automatic proof systems, in which every set belongs to a Grothendieck universe.
The concept of a Grothendieck universe can also be defined in an [[elementary topos]].<ref>

==Properties==
As an example, we will prove an easy proposition.

:'''Proposition'''. If <math>x \in U</math> and <math>y \subseteq x</math>, then <math>y \in U</math>.

:''Proof''. <math>y \in P(x)</math>  because <math>y \subseteq x</math>. <math>P(x) \in U</math> because <math>x \in U</math>, so <math>y \in U</math>.

It is similarly easy to prove that any Grothendieck universe <math>U</math> contains:
* All [[singleton (mathematics)|singletons]] of each of its elements,
* All [[Cartesian_product#Infinite_Cartesian_products|product]]s of all families of elements of <math>U</math> indexed by an element of <math>U</math>,
* All [[disjoint union]]s of all families of elements of <math>U</math> indexed by an element of <math>U</math>,
* All intersections of all nonempty families of elements of <math>U</math> indexed by an element of <math>U</math>,
* All functions between any two elements of <math>U</math>, and
* All subsets of <math>U</math> whose [[cardinality]] is an element of <math>U</math>.

In particular, it follows from the last axiom that if <math>U</math> is non-empty, it must contain all of its finite subsets and a subset of each finite cardinality. One can also prove immediately from the definitions that the intersection of any nonempty class of universes is a universe.

== Grothendieck universes and inaccessible cardinals ==
There are two simple examples of Grothendieck universes: the empty set and the set of all [[hereditarily finite set]]s.

Other examples are more difficult to construct.  Loosely speaking, this is because Grothendieck universes are equivalent to [[Inaccessible cardinal|strongly inaccessible cardinal]]s.  More formally, the following two axioms are equivalent:

: (U) For each set <math>x</math>, there exists a Grothendieck universe <math>U</math> such that <math>x\in U</math>.
: (C) For each cardinal <math>\kappa</math>, there is a strongly inaccessible cardinal <math>\lambda</math> that is strictly larger than <math>\kappa</math>.

To prove this fact, we introduce the function
:<math>\mathbf{c}(U) := \sup_{x \in U} |x|</math>,
where by <math>|x|</math> we mean the cardinality of <math>x</math>.  Then for any universe <math>U</math>, <math>\mathbf{c}(U)</math> is either zero, <math>\aleph_0</math>, or strongly inaccessible. Assuming it is uncountable, it is a [[limit cardinal|strong limit cardinal]] because the power set of any element of <math>U</math> is an element of <math>U</math> and every element of <math>U</math> is a subset of <math>U</math>. To see that it is regular, suppose that <math>c_\lambda</math> is a collection of cardinals indexed by {{mvar|I}}, where the cardinality of {{mvar|I}} and of each <math>c_\lambda</math> is less than <math>\mathbf{c}(U)</math>. Then, by the definition of <math>\mathbf{c}(U)</math>, {{mvar|I}} and each <math>c_\lambda</math> can be replaced by an element of <math>U</math>. The union of elements of <math>U</math> indexed by an element of <math>U</math> is an element of <math>U</math>, so the sum of the <math>c_\lambda</math> has the cardinality of an element of <math>U</math>, hence is less than <math>\mathbf{c}(U)</math>. 

By invoking the axiom of foundation, that no set is contained in itself, it can be shown that <math>\mathbf{c}(U)</math> equals <math>|U|</math>; when the axiom of foundation is not assumed, there are counterexamples: we may take for example <math>U</math> to be the set of all finite sets of finite sets etc. of the sets <math>x_\alpha</math> where the index <math>\alpha</math> is any real number, and <math>x_\alpha=\{x_\alpha\}</math> for each <math>\alpha</math>. Then <math>U</math> has the cardinality of the continuum, but all of its members have finite cardinality and so <math>\mathbf{c}(U) = \aleph_0 </math> (see Bourbaki's article for more details).

Now let <math>\kappa</math> be a strongly inaccessible cardinal. Say that a set <math>S</math> is strictly of type <math>\kappa</math> if for any sequence, we have <math>s_n\in\cdots\in s_0\in S</math>, with <math>|s_n|<\kappa</math>. (<math>S</math> itself corresponds to the empty sequence.) Then the set <math>u(\kappa)</math> of all sets strictly of type <math>\kappa</math> is a Grothendieck universe of cardinality <math>\kappa</math>. For details, again refer to Bourbaki's article, listed in the references.

To show that the large cardinal axiom (C) implies the universe axiom (U), choose a set <math>x</math>. Let <math>x_0=x</math>, and for each <math>n</math>, let <math>x_{n+1} = \textstyle\bigcup x_n</math> be the union of the elements of <math>x_n</math>.  Let <math>y = \textstyle \bigcup_n x_n</math>. By (C), there is a strongly inaccessible cardinal <math>\kappa</math> such that <math>|y|<\kappa</math>. Let <math>u(\kappa)</math> be the universe of the previous paragraph. Then <math>x</math> is strictly of type <math>\kappa</math>, so <math>x\in u(\kappa)</math>.  To show that the universe axiom (U) implies the large cardinal axiom (C), choose a cardinal <math>\kappa</math>. <math>\kappa</math> is a set, so it is an element of a Grothendieck universe <math>U</math>. The cardinality of <math>U</math> is strongly inaccessible and strictly larger than that of <math>\kappa</math>.

In fact, any Grothendieck universe is of the form <math>u(\kappa)</math> for some <math>\kappa</math>. This gives another form of the equivalence between Grothendieck universes and strongly inaccessible cardinals:

:For any Grothendieck universe <math>U</math>, <math>|U|</math> is either zero, <math>\aleph_0</math>, or a strongly inaccessible cardinal. And if <math>\kappa</math> is zero, <math>\aleph_0</math>, or a strongly inaccessible cardinal, then there is a Grothendieck universe <math>u(\kappa)</math>.  Furthermore, <math>u(|U|)=U</math>, and <math>|u(\kappa)|=\kappa</math>.

Since the existence of strongly inaccessible cardinals cannot be proved from the axioms of [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory]] (ZFC), the existence of universes other than the empty set and <math>V_\omega</math> cannot be proved from ZFC either.   However, strongly inaccessible cardinals are on the lower end of the [[List of large cardinal properties|list of large cardinals]]; thus, most set theories that use large cardinals (such as "ZFC plus there is a [[measurable cardinal]]", "ZFC plus there are infinitely many [[Woodin cardinal]]s") will prove that Grothendieck universes exist.
